newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovans hope for decent life after poll.
newsitem.headline: Moldovans hope for decent life after poll.

text.p: Moldova's presidential election campaign entered its last day on Saturday with expectations of a high turnout from its impoverished people who hope for at least a tiny change for the better.

In this bleak village some 20 km (12 miles) away from the capital Chisinau unpaved roads are clogged with mud, salaries and pensions have not been paid for months and food shops have no buyers because villagers have no money.
A dozen people spoke to by Reuters all said they would take part in Sunday's vote for the sake of a brighter future.
"Surely I will vote tomorrow, because there is no way to live like this any longer," said Irina, a young woman.

Moldova's three top leaders, President Mircea Snegur, Parliamentary Chairman Petru Lucinschi and Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, are the front-runners but political analysts predict a runoff between the two top contenders on December 1.

Sangheli presents himself as a man of few words but many deeds. He has close ties with Russia, Moldova's main market and fuel supplier which also has a military presence in the country's breakaway Dnestr region.
Experts say he is most strong in his native north and the south of the mainly agricultural state of 4.3 million people.
But in Magdacesti and the neighbouring village of Stauceni a vast majority of the people seemed to favour Snegur with Lucinschi also canvassing some support.
"There must always be hope...I would like Snegur to stay," said Ion, a middle-aged unshaven man in a worn-out leather jacket.

Villagers survive thanks to their garden plots on the fertile land. Despite hardships, most are friendly and good- natured, probably due to their most prized product -- very good wine produced in huge amounts by every household.
Snegur, 56, has led an aggressive and populist campaign, cultivating an image as "one of us".

His message was "I need more power to get things done" and he has vowed to dismiss the "corrupt" government and parliament and to change the constitution, turning Moldova into a presidential republic.
"I would like a firm hand, and at the same time a man who is with the people," said Eugenia, a private shop-keeper.
But Constantin, a village doctor, said he backed Lucinschi. "I will vote for Lucinschi...Snegur is a good man, but Lucinschi is better."
The more educated seem more likely to follow Lucinschi, 56, who is running as an independent. He presents himself as a moderate social democrat whose top priority is civic peace.
"Snegur and I have completely different positions," Lucinschi told a news conference in Chisinau on Saturday.
He added that Snegur's plans to amend the constitution and gain more powers could "drag the country into a circle of confrontation and tension".

Unlike Sangheli who leans towards Russia, Snegur favours closer ties with the West and also with Romania, which shares Moldova's language and culture. Lucinschi says his position "is just in between the two".
"If the president wins, Moldova might swing to the right. If the winner is the prime minister, it may shift to the left. I stand for good ties with all countries," Lucinschi said.
Despite predictions of a high turnout some people appeared to have given up all hope in Magdacesti.
"I haven't had my pension for eight months, and will not vote at all. I only want God to descend to Earth and be our president," said an old peasant.
